articles.title: This Friday in St Helens: Learn to Save Seeds and Share Them Locally
articles.body:
A community seed-saving and botanical art workshop is taking place at Chester Lane Library, Four Acre Lane, St Helens, on Friday 16 October 2026, from 11am to 12.30pm. Green Town St.Helens is organising the session, with Emma from Emma’s Wild Garden leading the activities.

Visitors can learn how to collect and store seeds, decorate their own seed packets and contribute seeds to the Chester Lane Seed Library, helping other local gardeners grow flowers and food in future seasons. Beginners are welcome. The organiser asks for a £5 booking deposit, refunded when you attend; spaces are limited, so check availability before travelling.

KS Garden Services tip: Only save seeds from healthy, mature plants. Allow seedheads to dry, label envelopes with the plant name and collection date, and store them somewhere cool and dry. Not every hybrid variety will grow true to its parent.

Photograph: Making seed packets, Pacific Southwest Region USFWS (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: RHS Bridgewater Trial Reveals Standout Hydrangeas for Autumn Colour
articles.body:
After five years of testing at RHS Garden Bridgewater in Greater Manchester, the Royal Horticultural Society has published its 2021–2025 trial results for Hydrangea paniculata. Twelve cultivars gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit, including BONFIRE, PASTELGREEN, REDLIGHT and SKYFALL.

The trial looked at plant health, vigour, flower colour and shape, and how well different varieties performed. Panicled hydrangeas are known for large, cone-shaped flowerheads that often change from white or green towards pink as they age, bringing interest from late summer into autumn.

For local gardens, the RHS advises planting in spring or autumn in moist but well-drained ground. Light shade works well, though a sunnier position can suit plants where the soil does not become too dry. The soil does not need to be acidic. Pruning last year’s growth in early spring can encourage larger flowers, but severe pruning is not essential for every garden.

KS Garden Services tip: Choose a hydrangea for its eventual size as well as its flowers. This avoids unnecessary hard cutting every year.

Photograph: Hydrangea paniculata (illustrative, not a named trial winner), Max071086 (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: STIHL's ALLPRO Batteries: Faster Charging for Professional Gardeners
articles.body:
Battery garden machinery continues to develop, and STIHL's ALLPRO system highlights just how quickly professional charging technology is moving. STIHL says its ALLPRO Performance batteries can reach 80% charge in as little as nine minutes when used with the AL 1802 MO high-speed charger under the specified conditions.

That headline figure applies to particular ALLPRO Performance batteries rather than every battery in the range. STIHL also states that the new ALLPRO batteries work with existing AP System tools, while charging speed depends on the battery and charger combination.

For garden maintenance businesses, quicker charging may eventually reduce the number of spare batteries needed on long jobs. However, equipment cost, weather resistance, battery weight and genuine run time still matter as much as the advertised charging speed.

KS Garden Services tip: Before buying battery equipment, check the exact tool, battery and charger combination rather than comparing headline charging times alone.

Photograph: Example of a cordless hedge trimmer (Makita model, not STIHL), Mark Hunter (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: North West Bird Watching Festival Returns to Martin Mere This Weekend
articles.body:
WWT Martin Mere near Burscough will host the North West Bird Watching Festival on Saturday 17 and Sunday 18 October 2026. The event celebrates autumn migration, when pink-footed geese and other wetland birds gather across the reserve.

The programme includes talks, guided walks, wildlife photography and opportunities to see species such as pintail, shoveler and pochard. WWT says visitors may see thousands of pink-footed geese moving between their roosting and feeding grounds. Check the official programme and ticket details before travelling.

Although a garden is very different from a wetland reserve, both benefit wildlife. In local gardens, seedheads, berry-producing shrubs and safe sources of water can help visiting birds through the colder months. Keep water clean and avoid disturbing sheltered habitats unnecessarily.

KS Garden Services tip: An autumn tidy-up does not have to mean stripping every border bare. Leave selected stems and seedheads where they will be attractive, safe and useful to wildlife.

Photograph: Pink-footed geese in flight in Lancashire, Apricaria (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: David Domoney's October Plant Picks: Flowers, Berries and Autumn Foliage
articles.body:
TV gardener David Domoney has shared his October 2026 selection of plants that can keep gardens colourful as the season changes. His recommendations include Heuchera villosa 'Autumn Bride', Mahonia 'Jungle Whisper', Pyracantha 'Saphyr Jaune' and Acer griseum.

These plants show that autumn interest is about more than late flowers. Heuchera 'Autumn Bride' carries airy white flower sprays over attractive foliage, mahonia can provide architectural leaves and flowers, pyracantha offers colourful berries, and paperbark maple (Acer griseum) is prized for peeling cinnamon-brown bark and autumn leaf colour.

Plant choices should match the garden's soil, light and space. Some larger shrubs and trees are not suitable for a very small border, while thorny plants need careful positioning beside paths and play areas.

KS Garden Services tip: For a garden that looks good for longer, combine flowering perennials with plants chosen for foliage, bark and wildlife-friendly berries.

Photograph: Heuchera villosa 'Autumn Bride', Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: Still flowering in October? Meet the Cornish lily!
articles.body:
Just look at that splash of pink! While many summer flowers are starting to fade, the Cornish lily (Nerine bowdenii), also called Bowden lily, comes into its own during autumn.

Its distinctive, curled petals can brighten borders in September and October — proof that the garden still has plenty to offer long after summer ends.

How to grow Cornish lilies:
• Position: choose a sunny, sheltered spot.
• Soil: free-draining soil helps bulbs thrive, particularly over winter.
• Planting: avoid burying bulbs too deeply — leave the neck exposed in a suitable sheltered position.
• After flowering: remove spent flowerheads and let the leaves die back naturally.
• Best tip: leave established clumps undisturbed for a good display in future years.
